⚠ Research Disclaimer
Independent research — not affiliated with KTM AG or Bajaj Auto. All analysis uses publicly available specifications supplemented by engineering estimates where OEM data is unavailable (marked ~).

On piston commonality: Whether the 399 and 349 LC4c share the same piston is not publicly confirmed. If they do, this analysis shows the shared unit operates comfortably within structural limits for both applications — a positive outcome. If KTM or Bajaj develop variant-specific pistons in future, only teardowns and durability data will confirm the direction. Either way, both engines are designed to meet warranty obligations. Real-world engine failures are almost never a design problem — they are overwhelmingly the result of manufacturing tolerances, assembly quality, and maintenance history.

Material & modelling assumptions: OEM piston alloy unpublished — 4032-T6 used as working assumption (standard forged piston alloy at this displacement, used by JE, CP-Carrillo and equivalent suppliers). FEA reflects idealised static load cases. Manufacturing tolerances, surface finish knockdown, thermal fatigue interaction, ring groove fretting, and combustion pressure variability are not fully captured. Results are indicative of structural behaviour trends, not certification-grade analysis.

Conrod estimate methodology — same-λ assumption: The 373 LC4 conrod is confirmed at 92.2 mm, giving λ = r/L = 0.3254. Since KTM has not published conrod dimensions for the LC4c, both LC4c rods are estimated by holding λ constant at 0.3254. This yields L_399 ≈ 98.35 mm and L_349 ≈ 86.28 mm. Note the 349 is significantly shorter than the 399 rod — the dashboard previously assumed 98.3 mm for both, which was physically inconsistent. The same-λ assumption is a reasonable engineering prior (designers typically keep λ in the 0.30–0.34 range to balance primary/secondary forces and block height), but treat these as estimated. Any future OEM confirmation should supersede these values.

9B Static Structural — Pressure Load Only (Case A, Shared Geometry) No inertia — identical for both variants
Why a shared case? Both variants use the same 89 mm bore piston geometry with near-identical CRs. With inertia excluded, the applied crown pressure is identical — this case isolates the pure pressure response of the shared geometry.

On the missing static SF contour: The Safety Factor output captured for Case A was from the ANSYS Fatigue Tool (zero-based, Goodman) — it is presented in Section 9E. Static structural margin can be inferred directly: σmax = 205.55 MPa vs Sy = 255 MPa → static FoS ≈ 1.24 at the pin boss stress concentration peak; crown and skirt bulk remain well above 2.0.
Interpretation: Peak von Mises occurs at the gudgeon pin boss fillets — a stress concentration from the geometry transition and cylindrical support constraint. Below yield (255 MPa) throughout. Deformation peaks at the crown edge, zero at the pin bore — physically consistent. The crown surface itself shows low bending stress; structural work is primarily done by the boss-to-skirt webs.
9C Thermal Analysis — Steady State (Case B, Shared Geometry) Convection BCs — identical for both variants
Why convection instead of heat flux? Heat flux BCs require unambiguous outward surface normals. On complex piston geometry — underside ribbing, ring groove transitions, oil gallery entrances — ANSYS normal direction can be ambiguous and risk incorrect flux assignment. Convection BCs (h, T∞) are physically equivalent at steady state and sidestep this entirely.
Surfaceh (W/m²·°C)T∞ (°C)Physical Basis
Crown face (combustion)500650Combustion gas — LC cycle average
Underside / lower crown2000130Oil jet cooling — high h, bulk oil temp
Skirt outer500165Cylinder liner contact — oil film interface
Piston ring grooves800200Ring-to-groove heat path — mixed gas/oil
Temperature Distribution — Case B
Max: 276.47 °C (crown centre)  |  Min: 138.02 °C (pin bore / lower skirt)
Total Heat Flux — Case B
Max: 2.625 MW/m² (ring groove edges)  |  Min: 795 W/m²
Interpretation: Crown centre at 276 °C is within the safe operating envelope for 4032-T6 (strength knockdown becomes significant above ~300 °C). ΔT of ~138 °C across the piston height is consistent with oil-cooled gasoline singles in literature. Peak heat flux at ring grooves is expected — smallest contact area, highest flux density. No singularities at crown centre confirm adequate mesh quality.
9D Comparative Static Case — Pressure + Inertia Loading (Cases C & D) 399 = Case C  |  349 = Case D
What differentiates the variants? Shared geometry means pressure response is identical. The variant-specific load is piston inertia at peak RPM — applied as body acceleration in the negative cylinder axis (TDC reversal). 399 uses 8,000 rpm (chosen conservatively below its 8,500 rpm power peak); 349 uses 8,600 rpm (shorter stroke allows higher rev ceiling).

Higher-loaded variant: 399 LC4c. Margins are extremely narrow across all metrics — ΔσvM = 0.65 MPa (0.32%), ΔFoS = 0.005. This is expected: the 399 has a longer stroke, so despite a lower rev ceiling its r·ω² slightly exceeds the 349. Both values nearly cancel — confirming the design is largely governed by combustion pressure, not inertia, at these RPMs. Both variants are structurally sound. Minimum static FoS of ~1.24 at the pin boss concentration; bulk regions well above 2.0.

Goodman rationale: Piston loading is zero-based (0 → Ppeak each cycle, not fully reversed), so mean stress is significant. Goodman interpolates between the R = −1 baseline and Su to correct for tensile mean stress. More conservative than Gerber — appropriate choice here since the S-N baseline data is R = −1.

Fatigue Life — Min at 8,000 rpm (hours) ~54.9 hrs ~52.9 hrs Both far exceed real duty cycle —
Both variants demonstrate excellent fatigue life. Minimum life of ~26–27 million cycles occurs only at the pin boss stress concentration. Everywhere else the piston exceeds the 5×10⁸ cap. At sustained peak RPM — which is not a realistic street duty cycle — even the minimum-life pocket would take over 50 hours to exhaust. The 349 edges the 399 marginally, consistent with its slightly lower von Mises stress. Both designs are fatigue-sound under these load assumptions.
Fatigue Sensitivity — Available Life vs Load Scale Factor (399 LC4c)
Available Life vs Load Scale Factor — 399 LC4c (Case C)
Zero-based loading | Goodman correction | At 1.0× = 6.897 MPa + 22,446 m/s² inertia | Data: ANSYS Fatigue Tool sensitivity export
Reading this chart: X-axis = load multiplier on applied conditions (1.0× = simulation load). Y-axis = minimum available fatigue life (log scale). Below ~0.875× load, life plateaus at the 5×10⁸ cycle cap — effectively indefinite life. At 1.0× the minimum life is 2.633 × 10⁷ cycles. Since Ppeak = 6.897 MPa is a derived estimate, the ±10% band (0.9× to 1.1×) is the practically relevant range — life there spans ~43M to ~16M cycles, both well above any realistic street duty cycle. Life drops steeply above 1.0× — aluminium has no endurance limit, so overloads are punishing.
